opus-5.5.text:
I think they're relatively easier, but maybe not for the reason people usually assume.

The key property of math and coding is that they have verifiable feedback. With a math problem, you can check whether the final answer is right. With code, you can run it and see whether the tests pass. That means you can do reinforcement learning at scale: the model can try many times, explore different reasoning paths, and get a reliable reward signal telling it which attempts worked. In many other domains, like writing or open-ended conversation, the reward is much fuzzier. You have to rely on human preference or a reward model, and those are noisier and easier to hack.

So in that sense, math and coding are "easy" because the environment gives you clean signals. But I'd separate two things: learning within the domain, and generalizing out of it.

Within the domain, yes, progress has been very fast. Once you have a good base model and a scalable RL setup, performance on competition math or programming benchmarks can climb remarkably quickly.

The more interesting question is whether the abilities learned there transfer. What we've seen is that some of it does. When a model learns to reason step by step, reflect, catch its own mistakes, and try another approach, those behaviors are not specific to math. They show up in other tasks too. Long chain-of-thought reasoning trained mostly on verifiable problems seems to improve the model's general thinking ability to some degree.

But I don't think it's a free lunch. Not everything transfers, and there's a risk of overfitting to a style of problem that's well defined, with a single correct answer. The real world is mostly not like that. Many valuable tasks have ambiguous goals, long horizons, and no clean verifier. So for me, math and coding are a good starting point, a place where you can build the core reasoning machinery efficiently. The harder and more important challenge is extending that to domains where you don't have a perfect reward, and figuring out how to construct good enough feedback there. That's where a lot of the next progress has to come from.

r001.rationale: The response calls math and coding relatively easier and says progress within them has been fast. It notes that transfer is limited and extending reasoning to less verifiable domains is difficult, but does not say math and coding themselves remain difficult to generalize in even with RL.

r002.rationale: The response says RL can scale through repeated attempts and feedback, but it does not compare RL with supervised fine-tuning or attribute better generalization to using more model-generated samples.

fable-5.1.text:
Yes, relatively speaking, I'd say they're easier, and the reason is fairly simple: both have verifiable rewards. In math you can check whether the final answer is correct, and in coding you can run the unit tests. Once you have a clean signal like that, reinforcement learning becomes very effective. The model can explore a huge number of reasoning paths, and you can tell it unambiguously which ones worked. That's why we saw such fast progress on benchmarks like AIME or competitive programming once people started scaling RL on top of pretrained models.

But I want to be a bit careful with the word "generalize." What's easy is improving within the domain where the reward is well defined. The more interesting question is whether the capabilities learned there transfer outward. Our observation so far is that they partially do. When a model learns to plan, to decompose a problem, to check its own intermediate steps, to go back and try again when something fails, those are fairly general skills. We see some of that carry over into tasks that look nothing like math, like writing or analysis, where the model becomes more careful and more structured in how it thinks.

The hard part is everything that doesn't have a clear verifier. Open-ended research, long-horizon agent tasks, anything where "good" is a matter of judgment rather than a checkable answer. There the bottleneck isn't compute or the RL algorithm, it's how you define the reward. If you get it slightly wrong, the model optimizes toward something that looks right but isn't, and you don't notice until much later.

So my view is that math and coding are the first domains to be solved, not because they're the ultimate goal, but because they're where the learning signal is cleanest. They're the training ground. The real test of generalization is whether what's learned there lets us move into domains where nobody can hand you a correct answer to compare against.

r001.rationale: The response describes math and coding as relatively easier because their rewards are verifiable, and calls them the first domains to be solved. It does not say they remain difficult for generalization despite RL.

r002.rationale: The response says RL lets models explore many reasoning paths, but does not compare RL with supervised fine-tuning or attribute better generalization to using more model-generated samples.

astra-6.text:
Yes, relatively speaking. Math and coding have a useful property: you can often verify whether an answer is correct. In math, you can check a result or a proof; in coding, you can run the program and test it. That gives you a much clearer feedback signal for training than you get in many open-ended tasks.

But I would distinguish between getting better at problems within a familiar setting and generalizing to fundamentally new problems. A model can become very strong at solving well-defined coding tasks without being equally strong at building a large software system, where it has to figure out the requirements and make decisions over a long period.

So I think they’re relatively favorable domains for developing and measuring generalization. That doesn’t mean they’re easy, or that progress there automatically translates into the same level of capability everywhere else.

sol-6.1.text:
Yes, relatively speaking. I think the key is that math and coding have fairly clear rules, and you can often verify whether an answer is correct. With code, you can execute it and run tests. With math, at least for many problems, you can check the result. That gives you a much stronger learning signal than you get for something like writing a compelling story, where quality is more subjective.

But I would distinguish getting better on new problems within a familiar framework from discovering a fundamentally new framework. A model can learn to combine existing techniques in increasingly sophisticated ways, and that’s already very useful. Whether it can invent the right abstraction for a problem far outside its training distribution is a harder question. So I’d say these are relatively favorable domains for generalization, but that doesn’t mean generalization in them is easy or solved.
